#4860. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4858. Kashmir’s Textile Legacy Inspires a Sumptuous New Line of Home and Fashion Accessories

Few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair

“It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk shows. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a new brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection

The company debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

“What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” says Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”

#4856. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4849. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4845. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4843. 76 AD-Approved Interior Photographers in the Northeast

Grand staircases. Cozy breakfast nooks. Color-drenched walls. Their images are portraits of homes, capturing a space’s personality and highlighting the talents of its designer. Read on to meet AD-approved interior photographers in the Northeast (and, in many cases, beyond).

A beachfront home in Santa Barbara, California.

Classical proportions and carefully composed details give William Abranowicz’s interior photos the poise of a still life. His background as a fine art printer shows in images that reward looking beyond the statement furniture to the smaller objects around it.

This vibrant San Francisco home designed by Noz Nozawa is sometimes called “the Rainbow House.”

Brittany Ambridge makes colorful rooms shine and white rooms look luminous without losing the details that give them dimension. Her lighting approach draws on techniques learned shooting film, translating a home’s atmosphere whether the mood is airy and expansive, or bold and colorful. She has worked with talents including Jeremiah Brent, Nate Berkus, Charlotte Moss, and Gachot Studios.

The living room of Kate Upton and Justin Verlander’s penthouse in New York

Glassworks offers a kaleidoscopic moment in a moody dining room.

From established businesses to young brands, Tori Sikkema will not only photograph your projects, she’ll also support your branding through consultations that will tailor her shoots to meet specific needs and goals. Her aim is always to allow her clients’ design style to shine through while creating photographs that evoke a sense of place and feeling.

The Connecticut living room of Matthew Malin and Andrew Goetz

Having shot the likes of Maude Apatow, Malene Barnett, and Michael Imperioli for AD, Calcutta-born Ashok Sinha’s portfolio of architecture, interiors, and portraits also includes The New York Times, Bloomberg, and several other distinguished outlets.

A primary suite in Brooklyn designed by Young Huh.

Jacob Snavely’s interiors photographs give lofty ceilings and carefully planned sightlines their due, with clear views that explain a room’s layout. His still-life and portrait work offers designers a way to extend that story beyond the overall space.

A living room featuring a rug designed by Colin King for Beni Rugs.

Billal Taright’s eye gravitates toward sculptural objects, spare arrangements, and the space around them. Warm tones and considered framing lend even a shelf or mantel quiet presence. The New York photographer moves between interiors, fashion, and collectible design, with Ralph Lauren Home, Colin King, and Luke Edward Hall also among his clients.

A kitchen by Jenna Chused of Chused and Co. for Isla Porter’s Tastemakers series.

Christian Torres makes interiors feel inviting and lived in, drawing on a practice that also spans hospitality and travel. He can participate from concept and location scouting through styling and lighting, helping designers carry a cohesive idea through the shoot.

Pattern and pigment freshen a traditional sitting room

No design detail is lost on Lesley Unruh, a Tennessee native and alum of Domino. Unruh, who now lives in New York City, has worked with Anna Burke Interiors, Malene Barnett, and CeCe Barfield Thompson, among others.

The grand staircase in a historic Georgian home in Pennsylvania designed by Haldon House.

Jason Varney brings a painterly handling of light and a strong feel for color to restaurants, hotels, and homes. His food photography makes him particularly useful for hospitality projects where the atmosphere extends from the dining room to the table, but homes are always on the menu too.

An indoor/outdoor living area in Sag Harbor, designed by Garnett.DePasquale Projects.

Nicholas Venezia brings architectural training and eight years at Selldorf Architects to his photography. His process connects a project’s underlying ideas with its visual story, a valuable trait when a designer wants the photographs to communicate more than appearances.

A 1909 mansion in New Jersey belonging to director Ruben Fleischer, designed by Studio DB.

If Brooklyn brownstones and beautifully considered hotels populate your design daydreams, spend some time with Matthew Williams’s portfolio. His interiors photography moves between whole-room views and studies of furniture, materials, and smaller objects. His portfolio includes homes by Elizabeth Roberts and Studio DB, giving designers examples of how a project can unfold across a sequence of images.

Tour a strikingly modern home in East Hampton

A resident of New York City but available for work worldwide, Tim Williams captures a sense of life in his photographs of commercial and residential interiors. His images recently graced AD PRO’s coverage of David Thomas’s new Madison Avenue outpost for Manolo Blahnik.

The powder room of a West Village townhouse designed by Starrett Ringbom.

A veteran of the fashion industry, Regan Wood shifted her focus to architecture and interior photography some time ago. Still, she sees a connection between them in that both form an “outward expression of one’s inner life.”

#4840. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4839. 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad

They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

With Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill

Helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

The Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

Partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results.

A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates.

Simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban, and Olson Kundig, documenting buildings across New Zealand and beyond.

Joseph Dirand designs rooms; his brother Adrien photographs them, including the architect’s Paris apartment for AD. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior. A creative family, to say the least.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios

Having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands.

Some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in.

Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

Venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis, Vincent Van Duysen, Axel Vervoordt, and Massimo Adario, among others.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

Kenzo Takada’s Paris home is just one stop in Mitchell Geng’s portfolio. The Tokyo photographer also captured a colorful Hong Kong residence for Vogue Hong Kong and includes architecture, interiors, and hospitality in his photographic itinerary.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec

Whether she is shooting portraits, food, travel, or interiors, Sylvie Li’s commercial and editorial images build a narrative. Just look at how she commemorates the marriage of old and new in this renovated Montreal apartment which appeared in AD.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

If Laura Gonzalez, Hugo Toro, and Pierre Yovanovitch feature on your list of design heroes, Stephan Julliard’s portfolio warrants a visit. The Paris photographer has worked with all three, as well as Jean-Louis Deniot, Kelly Wearstler, and Greg Natale.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows

Having shot for Dimorestudio, MacGuffin, Icon, and—hello, AD—Kyle Knodell has a knack for producing interior photos filled with life. At AD, we’ve tapped him to photograph Samantha Angelo and Peter Ostrega in their LES home.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart

Fans of Ashley Montgomery, Sam Sacks, and Ali Budd may already have Lauren Miller’s images on their inspiration boards. The Toronto photographer captures interiors and still lifes, with work appearing in AD and House & Garden.

Balmore House in North London, designed by Studio 163

In AD100 designer Vincenzo De Cotiis’s 15th-century Italian palazzo, a breccia baixa marble was chosen for its resemblance to the palazzo’s original ceiling, shown in this bath along with a circa 1895 Carlo Bugatti chair.

A penthouse at One Park Drive, the Herzon & de Meuron building at London’s Canary Wharf.

Designer Jacques Garcia’s 17th-century apartment in Paris.

The bedroom of a New York townhouse designed by Greg Natale.

An apartment in Naples, Italy, designed by FADD Architects.

The guest bedroom in Tarek Shamma’s London apartment.

A London apartment designed by Douglas Mackie.

A private holiday home in Tuscany, Italy, designed by Vincenzo De Cotiis.

The kitchen in Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s home in Portugal.

Historic Castle Howard in North Yorkshire, London

#4836. Did Zendaya and Tom Holland Buy a $10.8 Million Home?

Zendaya and Tom Holland may have tied the knot, but they’re still marking new milestones together. The actors have reportedly purchased their first piece of real estate together. The Daily Mail broke the news, alleging that the Spider-Man co-stars paid about $10.8 million (£8.25 million) cash for a five-bedroom house in an undisclosed London suburb described as “exclusive” and “leafy.”

There are few publicly known facts about the property—which isn’t much of a surprise, considering it took months for the notably private couple to confirm that they had gotten married. While AD could not independently confirm the purchase, reports say that the stars scored a sizable discount on the property, which was listed with a price tag of $11.8 million (£9 million).

Per the Daily Mail’s reporting, the 5,000-square-foot dwelling sits on a one-acre plot and features four bathrooms and four reception rooms. “My youngest is very excited that Spider-Man is going to be living across the street,” an inhabitant of a neighboring home told the Daily Mail. “I told him, ‘You will have to kick a ball a long way to reach their back garden.’ I doubt they will have a housewarming party.”

Since 2018, Holland has owned a six-bedroom home in Kingston-upon-Thames in southwest London. He paid $3.35 million (£2.5 million) for the six-bedroom residence, which he extensively renovated from 2020 until 2023, when Zendaya reportedly moved in. The Dune star maintains several properties stateside: a $1.4 million five-bedroom, five-bathroom Mediterranean-style house near Los Angeles; a 5,000-square-foot, ranch-style home in Encino, California, for which she paid $3.97 million; and a $4.9 million three-bedroom condo in Brooklyn’s luxe Quay Tower.

#4834. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4833. The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU

Blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is currently priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

Once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she says.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

The living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

“That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh says. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co

While modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he says. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

While the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” says Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”

#4830. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the big screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” says Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

“I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” says Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”

Haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

The stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety shows, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch says.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence says of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”

While District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the new location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

The upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

The Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

The set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch says. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”

The library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch says. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I said there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”

Designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”

Lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” says Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson says. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”

#4829. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.
