#4754. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4753. Can AI Companions Really Help Us Feel Less Lonely?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As more and more people turn to artificial intelligence platforms such as ChatGPT for a wide range of applications, researchers are now asking whether the digital relationships they can provide might also meet our need for social connection.

For most of us, simple friendship is having someone to talk to, share experiences with, and turn to when things go wrong. Whether this friendship has endured for decades or involves someone we met recently, having a social connection can be invaluable, even as we grow older and more isolated. But what if the “friend” isn't actually human? Since the introduction of large language models and conversational artificial intelligence, ChatGPT and other services have become part of everyday life. Millions of people have already turned to AI chatbots for answering basic questions about everything from financial planning to medical concerns. Many people also ask for help with personal problems and look to these tools for emotional support and companionship.

Certainly, AI chatbots offer advantages when human contact is unavailable. They're available anytime, day or night, and you don't have to set up a meeting, worry about interrupting, or fear being judged for any personal confessions you make. Users can also keep talking for as long as they want without worrying that the chatbot will end the session early.

For people dealing with loneliness, this kind of care can be a tremendous source of comfort. But could having an AI pal make loneliness worse? This is a worry, especially for people dealing with psychological issues that require professional (human) help. An article recently published in the journal Translational Issues in Psychological Science addresses many concerns about social chatbots. In the article, researchers Zehra Merve Kaya and Edanur Kanbur at Boğaziçi University in Turkey present results from numerous studies into artificial companionship and how it can function as an alternative to the human social relationships we depend on. They conclude that artificial companions can help reduce loneliness, but only temporarily and to a limited extent.

Loneliness is much more than simply being alone. Many people enjoy solitude without feeling lonely; others may have extensive social connections but still feel their emotional needs aren’t being met. For them, having numerous friends, supportive families, and an active social life might still leave them feeling incomplete. Ultimately, loneliness is defined by the gap between perceived and desired social bonds. And it is far more common than you might think. According to a 2025 WHO report, one in six people surveyed globally reported feeling lonely, often for long periods. Being chronically lonely has been associated with medical and psychological problems, including depression, heart disease, cognitive decline, and premature death. Though most commonly associated with old age, loneliness can strike at any age. Surveys of adolescents and young adults suggest high levels of loneliness, despite social media and other online communication.

So, can artificial intelligence make a difference? Modern chatbots can display empathic statements, handle personal disclosures, ask follow-up questions, and otherwise respond in ways that mimic social contact and make lonely people feel heard and understood. Along with always being available, AI chatbots can also provide someone to talk to during a sleepless evening. People dealing with social anxiety can often view chatbots as a way of avoiding many problems with human connection. That includes the fear of embarrassment and rejection, as well as building a sense of trust. Still, when you interact with a (live) friend, your shared experiences often shape their response to a cry for help. That includes memories, emotions, and your shared understanding of your joint connection. Even when the friend doesn’t know what to say, that concern still comes through, along with the sense of being acknowledged by someone with their own ideas, feelings, and wants. Relationships are based on shared experience, disagreement, compromise, and trust.

AI is changing rapidly. Chatbots have evolved to extended, natural conversations, and future versions may become even better at memorizing personal details, responding to emotions, and adapting to humans. Whether this technology helps with loneliness or creates other problems remains unclear. Kaya and Kanbur note that most of the evidence they have presented has not yielded clear results (thus far). While AI companionship can help many people, too many questions remain unanswered to recommend it as a widespread option.

True friendship is more than talking with a perpetually upbeat companion that may not really understand what you are saying. We also need to form ties with others with various lives and experiences that may challenge our perspective. These relationships matter because they require effort to maintain.

While artificial intelligence can imitate many qualities of companionship convincingly, it cannot form an emotional bond. That is what makes human relationships unique. Ultimately, artificial intelligence is not a substitute for human contact, though it may work as a helper in the short term. Whether it cures loneliness or keeps people apart is still an open question.

Kaya, Z. M., & Kanbur, E. (2026). Artificial intelligence as a social substitute in loneliness. Translational Issues in Psychological Science. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/tps0000547

#4752. Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.

On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027

The reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of plan, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

And the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

Some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

The most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”

That’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t announced a single new consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that launched in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

The pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car plans for Robotaxi in 2024. No new consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Tesla is becoming a company that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

#4751. Ghosts don’t scare German shepherds

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 PM EST

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” said Lindblad-Toh.

From there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

“We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh said. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”

In some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

#4750. The Best Way to Respond After a Fight

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Comedian Brian Gaar has said, “Relationships are mostly you apologizing for saying something hilarious.” He is right that relationships involve differences about what is hilarious, and that partners need to apologize. People are human, with the weaknesses and differences that are part of life. Every couple gets off course at times, which can lead to each person becoming more attached to their position, resulting in a heated back-and-forth over who is correct. Proving a point can become more important than stopping the harm that is piling up.

Marriage researcher John Gottman has said that some fighting couples get trapped in the roach motel, where, as the old advertisement put it, “they get in, but they can’t get out.” These relationship “disasters,” as he calls them, contrast with relationship “masters” who have figured out how to either stop, calm down, or focus on solutions. One therapy approach calls this ability to exit damaging situations “workability.” This is a focus on what helps, instead of worrying about who did what. It may be true that the other acted like a toddler, slamming the door and stomping feet, but it might be more workable to focus on what would improve the current mood. It may be accurate to say they were wrong in the facts about what your mother actually said, but is that helpful to argue about? Is it moving the relationship forward? In throwing out opinions about who is right and wrong, it is good to consider the old advice: Is it true? Is it kind? Is it necessary? And, is it workable? Workability does not ask, “Who is right?” but “What is the right thing to do?”

One of the most workable actions in a relationship is a repair attempt. Time will heal many wounds, but injuries heal faster with treatment. This can happen in a kind conversation that contains conciliatory efforts. One study looked directly at the power of healing gestures. People filled out questionnaires and described incidents in which they had recently been hurt. The researchers followed participants for several weeks to find out what the offender did to make things right. Some did nothing, but others apologized, made recompense, and had a peacemaking attitude. The more steps the offender took, the more the other forgave. Positive attempts changed the way that the hurt person viewed the relationship and the other. Trying to make things right is almost always a step in the right direction.

Couple therapist and researcher Sue Johnson offers guidelines for addressing injuries that are not healing on their own. First, partners should speak about the hurt honestly and simply. This should focus on the feelings, not the fault of the one who caused it. The listening partner acknowledges the pain without getting defensive or excusing themselves. Second, the injurer needs to take ownership of what they did. This needs to be done without downplaying what happened. A real apology is needed, not a "Sorrrrreeee! Sheesh!” Even if the offender doesn’t agree on every particular—and they probably won’t—it is important to not get stuck rehashing details. Instead, partners should converse about what needs to be done next. This can be done by focusing on underlying needs, such as safety, responsiveness, and connection. This will provide a sense of moving forward and is reassuring. If couples can talk through the events without getting upset, it helps rework the memory into a less bitter version.

It is important to nurture and treat wounds, but that doesn’t fix things immediately. Someone can apologize profusely for breaking another’s arm, but the pain will still last for a while. The person who caused the injury has to allow this and not get frustrated: “I said I was sorry, just go use your arm already!” They also must feel regret for the pain, not just the problems it has created. Sincere apologies help couples recalibrate and commit to do better. The next time you say something hilarious but unhelpful, resist the urge to escalate. Try a sincere repair instead.

Harris, Russ, ACT with Love: Stop Struggling, Reconcile Differences, and Strengthen Your Relationship with Acceptance and Commitment (New York: New Harbinger Publications, 2009).

Michael E. McCullough, Eric J. Pedersen, Benjamin A. Tabak, and Evan C. Carter, "Conciliatory Gestures Promote Forgiveness and Reduce Anger in Humans," Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111, no. 30 (2014): 11211-11216.

Sue Johnson, Hold Me Tight: Seven Conversations For A Lifetime Of Love (New York: Little, Brown, and Company, 2008).

Adapted from Love Me True: Overcoming the Surprising Ways We Deceive in Relationships. Cedar Fort Publishing, 2016.

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The company said it “immediately” launched an investigation and corrected the issue so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.

BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 1:09 PM EST

One little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a big adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”

Black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4747. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4746. How to Navigate Seasonal Affective Disorder as a Couple

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As the weather cools and the leaves begin to change color, another change can occur: The depressed moods that come along with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) can begin to arise. SAD can do more than just dampen one’s mood in late fall and winter; it can also negatively impact one’s relationships. As fall arrives, one may want to get out and see the changing leaves, visit a pumpkin patch, or indulge in some holiday shopping. However, their partner may just want to crawl back under the covers and hibernate until the spring. Approximately 5% of people in the United States experience symptoms of SAD as the days grow shorter. Symptoms usually begin to show around mid-fall and carry on through the winter, beginning to relent around spring and summer. When one partner struggles with SAD, it can create feelings of frustration and resentment within the relationship. The fatigue, irritability, social withdrawal, and lack of sexual desire that can come with SAD may change how couples spend time together or interpret one another’s behavior. Here we discuss some practical ways to acknowledge our loved one’s feelings and SAD-related symptoms while still maintaining a connection and making room for how each person approaches the changing seasons.

SAD is officially defined as a major depressive disorder that has a seasonal pattern, following a regular cycle that typically begins and ends at the same time every year. People who experience SAD during the colder fall and winter months can have persistent low moods, low energy, sleepiness, changes in appetite, and a desire to withdraw from social activities.

The symptoms of SAD can be more severe than the “winter blues” that many of us deal with as the days get shorter and it gets darker earlier. For those who grapple with SAD, the activities of daily functioning are disrupted — and this can include their intimate relationships. Before judging a partner too harshly for what may seem to be a sudden mood change that comes as colder weather sets in, perhaps suggest that they meet with a professional to have an assessment done for seasonal affective disorder. Framing it as something psychological rather than assuming that one’s partner has lost interest in the relationship as a whole can help both partners approach the issue more productively.

SAD can have an impact on all aspects of daily life, from getting up in the morning to performance at work to interactions with the ones we love. This can create an imbalance when one partner is dealing with the negative effects of their SAD, and for the other partner, it is business as usual. SAD can lead to a decrease in motivation, which can look like disinterest from the outside looking in. One of the best ways to salvage a relationship when one person has SAD is to prepare before the symptoms set in. Focus on open communication between one another and ask questions such as “What kind of support feels most helpful when you are struggling?” or “How can we best stay connected when your energy is low?” Emphasize listening, sincere reassurance, and respectful communication over trying to solve a problem that may not be immediately solvable. The partner with SAD should come away from discussions feeling like their perspectives, needs, and opinions matter. For couples navigating seasonal depression, there are ways to connect when moods are low. The important thing to remember is to remain flexible. Suggest several options for time together, such as a short walk, a simple meal at home, or an affectionate touch that does not carry the expectation of sex. Be prepared to offer “low-energy” or “high-energy” versions of plans to work around the fluctuating symptoms of SAD. Offer invitations instead of hard and fast plans and try to stay away from statements that suggest the person needs to try harder to “break out of their seasonal funk.” It’s important in the relationship to support the partner with SAD without becoming their therapist. By keeping empathy and communication at the forefront, you can weather the seasonal depression period together.

Even the most well-intentioned partners can’t have all the answers. While keeping to a strategy of empathetic support and simple routines, seeking the advice of a professional can also go a long way in helping people with SAD. Treatment options such as psychotherapy, light therapy, and antidepressant medications can help people withstand the most challenging aspects of SAD until the symptoms begin to lessen as the days grow longer and the weather becomes warmer.

The colder months bring a lot of time for togetherness, from holiday parties to enjoying outdoor adventures in the snow. However, when a couple is navigating seasonal depression, the fall and winter seasons can look different. By sticking with small, flexible ways to stay connected and keeping the lines of communication open, couples can help make the season easier without allowing seasonal depression to define their relationship.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#4744. Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

“It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

#4742. 6 Signs Grand Theft Auto VI Is Coming Between You and Your Partner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has finally arrived, and many people are signing off from their lives and signing on to the virtual world. Set in the fictional, Florida-inspired state of Leonida, the latest installment takes you through palm-tree-lined streets, lavish estates, neon-lit nightclubs, and alligator-infested swamps. In this world, you can cruise in a sports car listening to a killer soundtrack featuring artists such as Tame Impala, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott, and PinkPantheress.

The graphics and attention to detail are remarkably realistic, making the experience immersive, even when painting your virtual bedroom in anticipation of your girlfriend coming home from prison.

In the weeks leading up to the release, it has been intriguing to see how frequently the excitement surrounding this game has made its way into my therapy sessions. So many people have talked about taking time off from work and booking hotel rooms so they can play uninterrupted. Many are considering skipping the holidays this year and spending Thanksgiving in Vice City rather than at the dinner table with their families.

As a couples therapist, I find this idea of disappearing into a virtual world fascinating, and to some extent, understand the appeal. Who wouldn't want to check out right now? Between geopolitical tensions and the threat of AI taking people’s jobs, reality hasn't been doing a great job of selling itself lately.

Entering a world where you don't have to worry about grades, respond to your mother's texts about the holidays, or figure out what to make for dinner while accommodating everyone's increasingly complicated dietary restrictions can be appealing. But when does checking out become a problem for your relationship?

Interestingly, at the center of GTA VI is the story of a couple, Jason and Lucia, who rely on one another to survive. Imagine spending hours navigating the complexities of a fictional couple's relationship while neglecting your own.

It’s remarkable how resourceful we become when we truly want something. Couples regularly tell me they’re too busy and too exhausted to plan date nights, weekend getaways, or even small, thoughtful gestures. Yet many of those same people somehow find bandwidth to take days off work, book hotel rooms, and clear their schedule for a video game.

A person may spend six hours tending to their virtual snake and re-stealing a car, but an hour of bedtime for their children feels like a waste of time. In Vice City, they have energy to strategize, learn from their mistakes, and keep trying, but when it comes to being emotionally available for their partner, they're ready to call it a night. Getting their relationship with Lucia from "Running on Empty" to "Hot Together" is worth an entire weekend, but planning an outing with their real partner requires three weeks' notice and a Google Calendar invitation. These are signs that focus on the game is having a negative effect on the real-world relationship.

Part of the appeal is that, in the game, the objectives are clear. Real relationships are messier. There are no YouTube tutorials walking you through every challenge or showing you how other people solved it. Still, if you can devote hours to mastering the complexities of repainting your car, finding new sunglasses, and stashing your weapon, some of that patience and determination can also be made available for the people in your real life.

If your partner is repeatedly calling you for dinner or your children are begging you to come see something they've been building, and these requests feel like inconveniences standing between you and your next engine upgrade, it might be worth examining what's happening.

Fascinating how buying flowers, answering texts, and remembering a girlfriend's preferences can become second nature to a person when a little heart pops up on the screen to celebrate, while managing these things in real life can feel like a difficult challenge.

It's important to remember that one of our most fundamental attachment needs is knowing that we can reach our partner and that they will respond when we need them (Johnson, 2008). When mundane attempts at connection generate responses of irritation or withdrawal, people will eventually learn to stop reaching out. Maybe initially, the peace and quiet can feel like a victory, but eventually, it will get in the way of what we really want, which is meaningful, loving, and connected relationships.

Booking a hotel room to spend three days playing a video game while your spouse drives your kids to soccer practice or plans your family's Thanksgiving meal is not a decision that just concerns you. Being in a committed partnership doesn't require relinquishing your personhood. It does, however, involve recognizing that your choices have consequences for other people.

Creating a couple bubble is about establishing a mutual agreement to protect and prioritize the relationship and look out for each other (Tatkin, 2012). It is healthy to want some space for our hobbies in our relationship, but when our leisure comes at our partner's expense, that will hurt the partnership.

In my practice, I see many couples whose romantic relationships gradually deteriorate into parent-child dynamics. One partner assumes more of the adult responsibilities. They begin monitoring screen time, reminding the other person of their obligations, managing household chores, worrying about their health, keeping track of bedtimes and meals, and making sure someone shows up to pick up the kids.

Meanwhile, the partner being "parented" feels criticized, controlled, micromanaged, and deprived of their freedom. This is not a healthy dynamic between adult partners.

The most alluring part of an alternate reality is that you can leave your emotional baggage behind. You don't have to process grief, worry about your aging parents, or think about the Christmas gifts you can't afford.

You can avoid difficult conversations about whether you're going to get married or try IVF treatment. And of course, unwinding is important to recovery, but before you know it, you can find yourself looking forward to your partner falling asleep so you can finally enjoy your evening by yourself.

You're working tirelessly to get your relationship with Lucia to "Hot Together" while your actual partner is wondering whether filing for divorce would finally unlock your attention.

The desire to escape isn't abnormal or shameful. We're overloaded and overstimulated. Real life is difficult, and our sense of agency is constantly challenged. However, it is valuable to understand what exactly it is that we are running away from.

As much as the desire to retreat into a different reality is understandable, we also could make our actual lives different, but of course, making real-life changes requires being present.

None of this means we can't enjoy the art, music, and unapologetically excessive world that GTA offers. But the real challenge isn't completing another mission; it's figuring out how to bring some of that same excitement, curiosity, and determination back into your relationship.

#4741. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, said in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That said, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

“In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#4740. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4738. How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

"Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley

How long should you wait before having sex? Moving in together? Getting married? These are among the most common questions people ask about romantic relationships. Yet there is no magical timeline that guarantees success. The value of waiting depends on the partners, their circumstances, and the nature of their relationship. Still, one principle often proves valuable: patience.

"Patience is not simply the ability to wait. It's how we behave while we're waiting." — Joyce Meyer

There's a crucial distinction between waiting and patience. Waiting is passive: Time passes while little changes. Patience, by contrast, is active. It involves investing in the relationship while recognizing that some developments should not be rushed. Patience creates the conditions for intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen naturally. Unlike procrastination, which unnecessarily delays action, patience reflects wise timing. The important question is not how long we wait, but whether we practice patience rather than merely let time pass (Ben‐Ze'ev, 2019; and here).

"I don't have a set time frame for sex, but it's always before it gets super serious. I've got to test-drive the car before buying it." — A woman

"My boyfriend and I had sex on the first date, and we're still together a year later and talking about getting engaged soon. The right person isn't going to think less of you because of the speedy sex." — A woman

Sexual attraction is a defining feature of romantic love, making the timing of sexual intimacy especially significant. Research often finds that couples who delay sex report greater relationship quality and lower breakup rates. Waiting may allow emotional intimacy and communication to develop before physical intimacy takes center stage. Some studies suggest that couples who wait several months before becoming sexually involved report greater satisfaction and relationship stability (Vancour & Fallon, 2017).

Yet these findings do not mean that sex on the first date is a mistake. What matters most is not the calendar but the context. Partners differ in their values, attachment styles, and goals. For some well-matched couples, early sexual intimacy may strengthen their initial bond. The important question is therefore not, "How many dates should we wait?" but "Are we both comfortable with the pace at which intimacy is developing?"

"With love and patience, nothing is impossible." — Daisaku Ikeda

Premarital cohabitation has become the norm for most American couples. Yet living together can serve very different purposes.

Research suggests that couples who move in together mainly to "test" the relationship are more likely to break up than those who cohabit because they genuinely want to spend more time together (Chapman et al., 2026). One reason is that living together creates practical and financial interdependence, making it harder to evaluate the relationship objectively. Couples who move in together after discussing long-term plans, or after becoming engaged, generally report better marital outcomes than those who simply drift into cohabitation because it feels convenient.

Researchers therefore distinguish between sliding into cohabitation and deciding to cohabit. Sliding involves little deliberate discussion or commitment; deciding reflects conscious consideration of the relationship's future. Indeed, more than half of cohabiting couples report that they had not explicitly discussed moving in together before doing so. The central issue is not whether couples should live together before marriage, but whether cohabitation expresses mutual commitment and thoughtful deliberation rather than uncertainty and inertia.

"The ideal amount of time to date before getting married is at least a whole year. It's crazy to marry someone before you've seen what they're like in winter." — A woman

No dating duration can guarantee marital success. Nevertheless, many relationship researchers and therapists suggest that two to three years often provides enough time to know a partner across different circumstances while preserving romantic momentum.

Dating typically differs from hooking up because it is part of a broader process of building an enduring relationship. Yet the distinction is far from absolute. Many successful relationships begin as casual encounters. One-night stands sometimes become lifelong partnerships, and dating apps such as Tinder, often criticized for promoting casual sex, have also become important pathways to marriage. The route matters less than what develops along the way.

"Lovers are patient and know that the moon needs time to become full." — Rumi

Love has no universally correct timetable. There are no strict rules governing when to have sex, how long to live together, or how long to date before marriage. What matters is not simply how long partners wait before taking the next step, but whether they use that time wisely. Passive waiting merely allows the clock to advance; active patience allows intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen. Romantic flourishing depends less on the passage of time than on what partners do with it.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The Arc of Love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Chapman, C. L., Liu, D. Y., Stanley, S. M., & Rhoades, G. K. (2026). Thinking about moving in together? Reasons for cohabitation are associated with relationship outcomes over time. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 15, 138-151.

Vancour, J. M., & Fallon, M. (2017). Romantic satisfaction in young adults as a function of sexual debut. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 22(2).‏
